content.thinking:
I need to write this entire file in one pass without iterative feedback, so I should plan the elephant's design carefully upfront: a low-poly African bush elephant at realistic scale, facing forward, with a skeleton starting from a pelvis root joint and extending through a spine chain toward the shoulders.

I'm mapping out the body proportions—shoulder height around 3.2m, belly clearance near 1m, body barrel as an ellipse roughly 1.6m tall—then plotting spine centerline points from rump to head base, with the head modeled as a large dome positioned above the neck to match an elephant's carried posture.

Defining spine joint positions...

Then I'll continue the spine chain forward from hips toward the chest, and build a separate tail chain running backward, before lofting the overall body as one continuous path with bone ownership split at the hips joint based on closest point along the curve.

I'll use piecewise linear interpolation for the radius profile and go with faceted, low-poly shading using 8-sided sweeps with smooth off for a flat-shaded look. Now I'm thinking about leg placement, with front legs positioned as columns from the shoulders.

For the legs, I'll treat them as nearly straight two-segment limbs with a slight bend to keep the total reach close to the actual leg length, bending front legs forward at the knee and back legs backward.

Hind legs bend forward at the stifle, so I'll keep that joint direction slightly forward too. Each limb returns three points that I'll name as hip/knee/ankle joints, placing left and right hips symmetrically at x=±0.5.

For the feet, I'm sizing wide low-poly cylinders with tapered radii along the leg (thicker at top, narrower near the ankle) so the thighs look appropriately thick and bulge slightly outside the body silhouette, which fits an elephant's proportions.

Now I'm adding toenails as small flattened boxes placed around the front of each foot, oriented to face outward using a direction and axis setting so they sit naturally on the foot's surface.

For the head, I'm planning a short neck chain connecting the spine to a head joint, with the skull shaped as a large ovoid form.

Now I'm shaping the ears as large, continent-like outlines extruded with slight thickness, attached to the sides of the head and angled outward and slightly back, with a plane oriented so width runs outward and height runs vertically.

Scaling the ear slightly larger and adding a hinge joint so it can be posed flared outward and back. For coloring, I'm writing a paint function that gives the ear a mottled grey base with pinkish edges toward the rim.

Adding vein lines radiating from the ear's attachment point using angle-based stripes, and planning a noise-driven wrinkle texture for the overall body skin to mimic elephant hide.

Still writing skin shader...

Bumping paintSize to 2048 gives finer texel density for crisper 2cm cracks without the texture getting too heavy. I'm thinking about squashing the y-axis in the crack cell noise to stretch cells into horizontal bands, mimicking elephant skin's natural wrinkle pattern alongside the cracked-mud look.

Now I'm roughing out the trunk as a chain of joints curving from the head down to near the ground, with the tip curling slightly forward — sketching out approximate control points along a ~2.2-2.5m length to get a natural resting pose.

Checking that the curled tip stays above floor level and setting a tapering radius profile from the thick base down to a thin tip, then planning to add wrinkle rings along the trunk for texture.

For the surface detail I'm sketching a paint function that creates periodic groove bands along the trunk's length using a fractional modulo pattern, blending it with the base skin color via smoothstep for soft edges.

I'm also planning the trunk tip features: a pair of small finger-like cone lobes, a dark flattened nostril ellipsoid, and tusks curving forward in ivory.

For the tusks, I'm sketching a sweep from the upper jaw root, curving down-forward then up over roughly 2.2 meters length, with a sequence of control points tracing that arc.

I'm splitting the mouth into separate upper and lower jaw pieces, with the lower jaw as a small tapering box hinged beneath the trunk base and angled forward-down, plus a visible lower lip. I'm setting up the jaw joint hinge location and aim direction, along with the head joint pointing slightly downward and forward.

Now I'm working out the body's vertical proportions in absolute world coordinates — foot height, leg column reaching up to the hip, body ellipse center and radius giving a back height around 3.1-3.3, and head/ear height bringing the total elephant height to roughly 3.4 meters.

Laying out the spine as a sequence of points from rump to chest, then assigning bone chain names across the three spans so the IK/FK rig has proper segments, with the final tip aimed along the end tangent before continuing into the neck chain points.

For the neck, I'm defining a short two-point chain with names for the joints, deciding the parent attachment should reference the spine chain's tip joint, and then placing the head joint with its own direction and role, before finalizing the neck's path and naming its last segment.

I decide to simplify by folding the neck into the body sweep bone, extending the body path up to the neck's end point, while the head gets its own separate loft. Writing body path points...

Defining radius profiles...

Skipping spine spikes but adding sparse bristle cards for the head crown and tail tuft, using a small tapered SVG polygon as the bristle texture. Now I'm plotting the tail chain starting at the rump root and curving down and back.

Still writing spike directions...

For the tail root, I need to make sure it attaches inside the body near the hips, and I should double check the rump geometry doesn't create weird gaps where the body's rounded cap ends versus where the tail begins.

Setting cap depth to 0.6 puts the rump around z=-2.3, and I place the tail root near [0,2.5,-2.25] with segments tapering down to [0,1.2,-2.5], keeping the root tucked inside the body surface to avoid any floating geometry.

Now I'm working out the hip joint position and leg attachment points - hind legs parented to the hips near z=-1.0 to -1.2, front legs parented to a spine joint further forward around z=0.75-0.8 to match the shoulder position, with leg root offsets set at roughly x=±0.55, y=2.0.

For the leg chain itself, I'm computing a two-segment limb reaching from the root at y=2.0 down to an ankle target near y=0.22, with segment lengths of 0.95 and 0.9 giving slight slack so the knee bends forward slightly for a natural elephant stance.

For the chain radius taper, I'm checking that the ankle cap and foot cylinder stay within the floor tolerance, verifying the bottom doesn't sink more than the allowed 2% margin.

Now I'm shaping the foot as a tapered cylinder covering the ankle joint, and picking a mottled dusty gray-brown tone for its color, tying it to the leg's tip bone.

Then I'm adding toenails as small ivory-grey boxes spaced around the front of the foot—five for front feet, four for hind—angled outward in even increments and positioned near the foot's edge.

Now I'm sketching the head shape: defining a sweep of path points from the base of the neck up to the trunk, with radii that taper from wider at the forehead to narrower near the trunk base, placing eyes along the side near where the trunk begins.

For the eye, I'll use a raycast hit to place a small dark iris sphere, plus a darker eyelid rim and a tiny white highlight sphere for shine, giving it a realistic wet-eye look against the darker brow area.

I'm also sketching twin forehead domes as ellipsoid bumps near the eyes, checking for valid raycast hits before placing geometry so nothing gets attached to empty space.

Now I'm checking the trunk's attachment point to the head—realizing the round end cap of the trunk's path geometry extends further than I expected, which could push it past the head's front surface and cause overlap.

Setting the trunk's path points to sweep forward and downward from the head, starting at a wide base of 0.3 radius so it looks naturally thick where it meets the face. I'm now checking whether the tusk base positions fall inside the head's elliptical cross-section so they don't awkwardly clip outside the surface.

I'm placing tusk points so they curve outward from the mouth, widening slightly to avoid overlapping the trunk, and tracking the total body length from tail to trunk tip, which comes out to about 6.3 meters. Next I'm figuring out where the ears attach along the head's curve.

Setting up ear orientation vectors...

I realize the ear is too tall relative to the overall head height, so I'm scaling the outline down by a factor of 0.9 and adjusting the attachment point so the top sits around 3.45 and the lower point around 1.7, keeping proportions sensible against the 3.8 total height.

Setting edge thickness so the ear is thicker near its base and thinner toward the top, with a small bevel for softness. For the outer face paint, I'm blending a base skin tone with radial vein patterns computed from angle and distance in the local surface coordinates, layering a rim highlight on top.

I'll blend in pinkish mottled patches near the ear edges using noise, keeping both ear faces painted the same. For the mouth, I'm placing the lower jaw as a tapered box section between the jaw joint and chin point, giving it a sharp low-poly look.

Positioning the jaw box beneath the head, then adding hair details: crown bristles, tail tuft, chin whiskers, and a few bristles near the trunk tip, scattering them across the head surface with distance constraints.

I'm also adding sparse body bristles over the back, since real elephants have scattered hair, using small narrow bristle cards with slight lean and bend for a natural look.

Now I want to add skin fold ridges around the leg joints, like wrinkle rings near the knees, by sweeping darker rings along loop paths at points on each leg's bone chain.

I'm weighing the cost of too many sweep rings against the visual payoff, deciding to scale back to just two leg-fold locations per leg (around t=0.45 and 0.7) rather than three, giving 8 sweeps total instead of 12, using pentagon cross-sections for the bands.

Elephants naturally have wrinkle bands near knees and ankles, so placing the fold loop near t=0.5 actually reinforces the joint look rather than risking a crash there. For shading, I'm planning to handle the belly and chest/hip countershading through paint based on surface normal rather than extra geometry, and settling on octagonal sides with flat faceting (smooth off) for the body parts, bumping to decagon for the main body. For the ears, I'm setting up a hinge joint parented to the head joint, positioning it around [s*0.42, 2.85, 1.7] with an aim target before building the ear mesh itself.

Now I'm setting up the ear's aim direction and starting to write the actual module: importing the builder, frame, rng, path, limb, paint, texture, and sweep utilities. I need to double check which imports actually get used in the final code to avoid unused-variable errors — dropping `frame` and `polyline` unless they end up needed — then defining the metadata object and starting the color constants for eyes, nails, and ivory tones.

Finishing the color palette with hair, pink, fold, and dust tones, then building the skin paint function. It blends base tones using noise, lightens undersides, adds dusty coloring near the ground, and uses a squashed cellular pattern to carve cracked skin textures into the surface, darkening the cracks.

For the trunk, I'm deriving its skin from the base skin paint but adding grooved segmentation along its length using a sawtooth pattern on the chain parameter, plus a pinkish tip tone blended in near the very end of the trunk.

Now I'm shifting to building the skeleton: setting up the builder and creating the hips joint as the root, considering giving it a forward-facing aim direction so the bone points along +Z rather than defaulting to +Y. Then I'm defining the spine chain as a catmull-rom curve through several points rising and arcing forward from the hips, parented to the hips joint with named segments.

Still writing joint hierarchy...

Setting up neck, head, and jaw joints, each parented appropriately with specific positions and aim directions, then starting to define a body sweep path using the same spine points plus an extra tail-end point, extracting the resulting knots for further processing.

Now I'm worried about mismatched array lengths between the interpolation knots and the radius arrays — if the knots and control points don't line up, the interpolation could produce NaN values, so I'm considering computing the parameter values directly from the path's closest-point function to guarantee ascending, matching indices.

Then I check that the radius direction convention is consistent, confirm faceted shading at 10 sides is acceptable, and move to defining the leg joints — setting root and foot positions per side so the limb segment lengths match the straight-line distance between them.

Still writing leg chain...

Setting leg radius tapering from thigh to foot, with flat end caps and smooth round starts blending into the body, using round cross-sections for a natural limb shape.

Calculating the foot's radius profile along its height to figure out where to place the toenails so they sit flush against the tapered surface.

Front nail angles set at -48 to 48 degrees, symmetric since both legs face +Z. Now adding fold loops along the leg surface at a few points along the sweep to create wrinkle detail.

That's 4 legs with 16 sweeps total, which should be fine without z-fighting issues. Now I'm moving to the tail chain setup, starting from the hip parent and defining its position.

Building the tail with 5 joints along a curve, tapering radius from 0.08 down to 0.025 with skin-colored hexagonal sweeps, then adding 9 hair-colored tuft spikes radiating from the tip at an angle.

For the head, I'm sweeping a curve through three points with varying radius profiles (rx and ry) to form an elliptical head shape bound to the head bone, checking that the head's front cap and rear sit correctly relative to the body depth so they don't clip awkwardly.

Then I'm adding two flattened forehead domes using scaled sphere geometry, adjusting their vertical position so the top matches up with the ear tops around height 3.36, keeping them bound to the head bone with a flat shading style.

Now I'm positioning the eye using a surface sweep around the head, calculating azimuth from the side flag so left and right mirror correctly, then placing a small embedded sphere for the eye and starting an eyelid ring around it.

Adding a small white gleam highlight on the eye with a tiny offset sphere, then thinking about adding a thin dark wedge stain beneath the eye for a temporal gland mark.

Elephants need long lashes, so I'm setting up a ring of lash spikes angled around the top of the eye using the bone ring helper, then starting to build the trunk as a chain of segments following a curved spline parented to the head.

Writing trunk sweep code...

Adding finger-like spikes at the trunk tip...

For nostrils, I'll use small flat dark cylinder discs oriented along the trunk direction and positioned slightly forward from the tip using the offset helper. Then I'm considering whether to skip trunk bristles or add scattered whisker cards along the top sweep near the base.

For tusks, I'm sweeping a curved spline through control points with tapering radius, giving them an ivory color base with colored bands near the tip to suggest scuffed and lighter ivory sections, using pointed end caps.

I'm adding a small collar piece at the tusk base to cover the root where it meets the gum, aiming it along the tusk's tangent direction so it blends naturally. Now I'm shifting over to defining the ear outline, starting to sketch its shape points for the extrusion.

Defining ear extrude parameters...

Checking how the ear attaches to the head geometry, making sure the ear root sits properly within the head's curvature so the back edges flare outward correctly without clipping.

Setting up the ear joint as a hinge parented to the head, then naming it per side. Now I'm sketching a bristle shape for hair on the head crown and configuring card parameters for lean, bend, and spin variation to scatter them naturally.

Now I'm defining scatter hits for the head and body surfaces with filters based on normal direction and position, and starting to build jaw geometry using tapered box sections for the lower jaw and mouth strip.

Checking the jaw against the trunk base's position so it stays mostly hidden behind the trunk but peeks out near the tusks—adjusting the jaw's start and end coordinates to shorten it slightly for a better fit.

Now I'm thinking about adding subtle surface detail like neck wrinkles and body fold bands using loop sweeps along the body surface, making sure to pass an explicit direction vector since a literal point won't default correctly for these loops.

For the body cross-section rings, I want to check which z-planes intersect the main body versus the legs, since loops need to wrap around a point that's actually enclosed by the surface. I'm planning a few sparse girth folds at select z-values to suggest elephant-like skin ridges without overdoing it, treating them like subtle barrel-hoop creases on the torso.

I'm settling on three neck folds near the shoulder region, each a thin raised loop with small radius and lift, tagged with a fold color, keeping the overall part and triangle counts manageable for the whole model. I also want to make sure the bone weighting for these sweeps correctly references the hips-spine-neck chain so the skin deforms properly, and I'm double-checking how the bone span calculations handle that joint sequence.

For the limb IK, I'm working out how to specify the bend direction argument—checking whether it accepts a single vector or needs to be wrapped in an array depending on the type signature, and leaning toward passing a bare direction vector based on the documented example.

For the chains, I'm setting up a polyline of points for each limb, defining front leg chains with a spine parent attachment and contact point options. Then I'm planning the skin sweep call with a radius profile for the legs, and thinking about adding haunch bulges as sphere shapes on the rump for the hips.

Now I'm writing the paint function for the ears, calculating vein patterns using angle-based noise, rim darkening near the edges, and blotch textures blended with the base color.

I'm checking the type signatures across paint callbacks and verifying import statements for all the helper functions I'm using—cells, mix, noise, smoothstep, interpolate, rng, catmull, limb, and the texture/builder utilities.

For the tail, I'm adding spike-based hair tufts at the tip using directional vectors and bone attachment, keeping the base point anchored to the tail's end position. I'll skip teeth, tongue, and mouth details since they aren't visible, and finish by returning the root builder object.

Now I'm sorting out type helpers for accessing the last joint in a chain, and setting up a hit-based eye ring where lashes are generated as small spikes radiating around the eye surface using angle and tilt parameters.

Confirming the stick/frame interface works with scale options, then I'll skip extra details like chest bulges or back ridges and move on to verifying foot placement at the ground plane before writing the file out.
